**A single straight cut turns the L-shaped floor into two rectangles whose areas can be added.**

The cut runs across the full 8 m width, giving a top strip 8 m by 3 m and a lower rectangle 5 m wide. Its depth is the rest of the 7 m left edge: 7 m − 3 m = 4 m. The parts share only the cut line and cover the whole floor.

accessibility.description: Explains the single straight cut that separates the L-shaped floor into a top 8 m by 3 m strip and a lower 5 m by 4 m rectangle, and why the cut is valid.

display.caption: The L-shaped floor plan with the single cut that separates the floor into two rectangles: the top rectangle running 8 m across and 3 m deep, and the lower rectangle 5 m wide with its depth obtained as 7 m − 3 m = 4 m.

display.label: Top strip, lower rectangle, and whole floor
display.condition: the two parts share only the cut line

accessibility.description: Shows the top strip area from 8 m × 3 m, the lower rectangle area from 5 m × 4 m, and the whole-floor area from adding 24 m^2^ and 20 m^2^.

display.caption: The floor plan split into the top rectangle and the lower rectangle, with the top rectangle carrying 24 m^2^ from 8 m × 3 m, the lower rectangle carrying 20 m^2^ from 5 m × 4 m, and the two part-areas added to give the whole floor, 44 m^2^.

display.title: Overall length times overall width
display.belief: I can find the floor's area by multiplying the overall length by the overall width: 8 m × 7 m = 56 m^2^.
display.evidence: But the floor is the two rectangles: 8 m × 3 m = 24 m^2^ and 5 m × 4 m = 20 m^2^, giving 24 m^2^ + 20 m^2^ = 44 m^2^. The extra 56 m^2^ − 44 m^2^ = 12 m^2^ is the 3 m by 4 m bottom-right region, not part of the floor.
display.conclusion: The floor's area is the two part-areas added: 24 m^2^ + 20 m^2^ = 44 m^2^. Multiplying the overall sides counts a 3 m by 4 m region outside the floor.

accessibility.description: Corrects the belief that overall length times overall width gives the floor's area by showing the 56 m^2^ product includes a 3 m by 4 m region outside the floor.

display.text: You have seen that the floor is not a single rectangle. Before we deal with that, the area rule for one rectangle needs to be solid. **The area of a rectangle is its length times its width, reported in square units.** Area counts unit squares, so the result is a number of square units such as m^2^, not a length.

accessibility.description: Recalls that the area of a rectangle is its length times its width, reported in square units rather than a length.

display.title: A split must not overlap or leave gaps
display.belief: I can split a shape into rectangles, add their areas, and it doesn't matter if the pieces overlap or if a bit of the shape is left out.
display.evidence: Suppose two rectangles both cover the same middle strip. Adding their areas counts that strip twice, so the total is bigger than the shape really is. The same thing happens when a corner is left uncovered: that region is counted zero times.
display.conclusion: The parts must not overlap, and together they must cover the shape exactly, so every region is counted once and nothing is counted twice.

accessibility.description: Corrects the belief that split pieces may overlap or leave gaps, explaining that each region of the shape must be counted exactly once.

display.title: A split that overlaps
display.belief: Any split works. Once I have two parts, I just add their areas, even when the parts sit on top of one another.
display.evidence: Read as a 5 m by 7 m left column and an 8 m by 3 m top strip, the floor gives 35 m^2^ + 24 m^2^ = 59 m^2^. Those two parts share the top-left 5 m by 3 m region, so 15 m^2^ is counted twice.
display.conclusion: The parts of a split must not overlap, because every region of the shape has to be counted exactly once. The correct split gives 44 m^2^.

accessibility.description: Challenges the belief that any split can simply be added: the overlapping split totals 59 m^2^ by counting the shared 5 m by 3 m region twice, while the non-overlapping split gives 44 m^2^.

display.caption: The floor plan with a 5 m by 7 m left column and an 8 m by 3 m top strip drawn as the two proposed parts. The 5 m by 3 m region where they overlap is marked as the region counted twice, and 35 m^2^ + 24 m^2^ = 59 m^2^ is compared with the correct 44 m^2^.

display.text:
A common belief is that the unit is just decoration, so 44 on its own is enough. A bare 44 does not say what was counted, and it could just as well be a length of the room's edge. Area is a count of unit squares, so the floor's area is written 44 m^2^.

Every area answer needs its square units attached. Whatever total you reach for the stage floor, write it in m^2^, because the number alone does not tell a reader what was measured.

accessibility.description: Explains why area is a count of unit squares and why a bare number cannot be read as an area, so the floor's 44 m^2^ and any stage floor total carry square units.
